ti: lint exits 0 when its path cannot be read, so a mistyped invocation passes CI while linting nothing

note: Not a defect. lint already returns 1 when spec.Load fails, and measuring without a pipe confirms it: lint -root . exits 1, lint /nonexistent exits 1, lint . exits 0. The original claim came from reading $? after piping stdout into head, which reports head's exit status rather than the program's. An implementer reported the symptom and the orchestrator confirmed it with that same flawed method, so the check agreed with the claim instead of testing it. Learning worth keeping: never read an exit code through a pipe; use PIPESTATUS or redirect instead. The only true part of the report stands — lint takes a positional path and -root is not a flag it accepts.

sum: bug lint exits 0 when its path cannot be read, so a mistyped invocation passes CI while linting nothing — DEFECT
body:
DEFECT
The lint subcommand takes a positional PATH. Given a flag-shaped argument instead, e.g. lint -root DIR, it treats the flag as the path, prints lint: lstat -root: no such file or directory, and exits 0. Reproduced on the shipped binary: stdout carries the error, echo $? reports 0. A CI step, Makefile target or agent script written with the wrong form therefore reports success while never linting a single spec file. The documented contract is the opposite: lint exits 1 on errors, which is why CI relies on it as a gate.

IMPACT
Silent, not loud. The failure mode is a green pipeline with no linting, which is strictly worse than a red one. This repository's own CI and Makefile happen to use the correct positional form, so nothing is currently unguarded here, but an agent copying the wrong form into a task template would disable the gate invisibly. Found by the T-01KYCT7KG8ED9BQMWA4FGME7QF implementer, whose task template carried the wrong form.

CAUSE
An unreadable path is treated as an empty walk result rather than as a hard error, so the zero-findings success path is reached.

FIX (decision at implementation)
A path that cannot be stat'd is a usage error: report it and exit non-zero. Consider also rejecting arguments that begin with a dash outright, since lint has no flags and a dash-prefixed path is far more likely a mistake than a real file name.

VERIFY
Regression test over the CLI: lint with a nonexistent path exits non-zero; lint with a valid path and a clean bundle still exits 0; the existing exit-1-on-findings behavior is unchanged.

ROLLBACK
One error path in the subcommand; reverting restores the current silent success.

ti: the resident server restarts itself when its binary goes stale: the last manual step after every merge becomes mechanical

note: serve -self-restart (opt-in, HTTP-only; stdio logs hint-only by design): a watcher polls Server.BinaryStale — deliberately mirroring the proven staleHint path byte for byte after a first draft judged s.main and never fired — and on staleness rebuilds IN THE SERVED TREE (Server.ServedDir; the second live defect: building in the CommonRoot-resolved primary checkout produced a replacement that did not know its own flags), renames atomically over the executable, drains, and execs with identical argv. The adversarial review then refuted the draft on exec semantics and four repairs landed: the swarm identity is carried explicitly in the exec environment with any pre-existing entry REPLACED never appended (defers never run across syscall.Exec so Deregister is skipped, and a fresh random agent would ghost-block its own pre-swap leases and orphan its worktrees; the append variant lost to a first-match empty entry in live proof), a drain timeout no longer aborts the swap (the binary is already replaced and the pidfile gone — exiting there vanishes the resident server, strictly worse than severing laggard streams; the drain error is logged and the exec proceeds), the rebuild is context-bound with a post-build ctx check so a stop signal racing a build wins instead of resurrecting the process, and the new image is backdated to the build START so a source edit landing mid-build reads stale to the replacement instead of being permanently missed. Live-proven twice: the full swap cycle (two serving lines, same port, replacement answers state) and identity continuity (identical agent set across the swap, server heartbeat fresh under the same name). Known limitations, accepted loud: a future-dated source mtime re-triggers swaps until wall clock catches up; the pidfile-and-port window during exec plus reindex can race a concurrent starter; two self-restarting servers sharing one binary path collide on the .new artifact — all logged, none silent. Process confession in the record: a reflexive git checkout reverted the implementation mid-iteration and it was restored from context, suite green before and after
